Writing this textbook has been an interesting personal journey. Two experiences motivated it, and many researchers at the interface of statistics, AI and astronomy will recognize both. First, I repeatedly discussed techniques with colleagues and often ended up scribbling LaTeX notes to share my thoughts. Over time, these scattered notes helped my collaborators, and they also helped me to organize and clarify my own understanding. Writing forces a clarity of thought that conversation does not give.

The second experience matters more to me. I have repeatedly been drawn into arguments about the usefulness of machine learning in astrophysics. In these arguments, “machine learning” often means different things to different people. The responses I encounter range from too pessimistic to unrealistically optimistic, and I find both positions difficult to defend.

These discussions touch on questions that go far beyond technical implementation. What does it mean for a method to be trustworthy? What makes something interpretable? Is deep learning always a black box? Are simpler models morally better? What is our philosophy of science, and what should be the ultimate goals of science?

I find these conversations fascinating because they show how much our choices of method rest on deeper beliefs about the nature of scientific knowledge. Writing this textbook has helped me organize my thoughts on these questions. It has also given me a more coherent view of the role of different statistical approaches in astronomical research. The process has been as much about understanding my own views as about communicating them to others.

An informal poll that I ran on social media encouraged me to start this project. The overwhelming support of colleagues convinced me to take it on. The step from scattered notes and lecture materials to a coherent textbook proved more demanding than I expected, especially for a non-native English speaker.

When I began this project, I ambitiously planned a single volume. It would cover both classical machine learning (Chapters 4 to 14) and deep learning (Chapter 15) in equal detail. This turned out to be wildly optimistic. The classical methods alone expanded to fill the current volume. I hope that I have given a sufficient introduction to neural networks and deep learning. A full treatment of these topics will need a separate volume, a project I look forward to once I have recovered from this one.

This has been one of my largest academic undertakings. From the first idea to the first draft, each page took about one hour of focused work. Many cups of coffee and the occasional dessert kept me motivated, and rounds of editing and revision added another hour per page. For the original 650-page version, the total time approached 1,300 hours. It consumed most of my free time and weekends during the 2024-2025 academic year.

Trimming the book to about 500 pages added another few hundred hours. The companion tutorials come from many years of my teaching, and curating them took another few hundred hours. Many of their examples are drawn from or inspired by my own research. This time commitment made me more sure that the deep learning volume should wait.

I should acknowledge the role that large language models (LLMs) played in making this project feasible. The preliminary writing, the organization, the mathematical content and the overall perspective represent years of my own thinking and research. The first draft of much of the lecture notes began in 2020, before LLMs, and I taught the course until recently.

I used LLM assistance mainly for language editing. It made the text as readable as possible while keeping my professional voice and, I hope, my occasional attempts at humor. Without this support, the language polishing alone would have made the project too time-consuming for a non-native speaker. The irony is not lost on me that a textbook partly about machine learning was itself made possible by machine learning.

I also thank David Weinberg for his enthusiastic support, his very careful reading of the book and his many insightful comments. I cannot believe that anyone would have the patience to read through such a gigantic volume, but David did.

My own research is on deep learning applications in astronomy. Even so, I remain convinced that a solid grounding in classical statistical methods covers a large part of the analytical needs of our field. Some astronomical problems do benefit from deep learning, and this is why I find the research area so interesting. Still, domain knowledge combined with solid statistical reasoning can solve many problems that first seem to need more complex approaches.

We should choose between classical and modern methods according to the nature of the problem, rather than fashion or technological enthusiasm. My goal is to provide the grounding needed to make such choices thoughtfully, knowing the trade-offs.

As I said in the preface (Chapter 1), I hope that this textbook adds depth to our understanding of how machine learning techniques have evolved. I also hope that it shows how they connect to the statistical ideas that astronomers have long used. If it contributes to more meaningful discussions about the role of these methods in astronomy, the considerable time investment will have been worthwhile.

Accessibility mattered to me from the start. I grew up in Malaysia, where educational resources in fields such as statistical astronomy can be hard to find. I know well how barriers to access can hold people back. I therefore chose to release this book on arXiv, freely available to anyone with an internet connection.

Later, Cambridge University Press came to me and, despite the arXiv version, was kind enough to want to publish the book. I am surprised by this interest and grateful for it, and it has led to the final published version.

This textbook is dedicated to my family, who supported my somewhat unusual intellectual path with great patience. My parents put up with a child who preferred solving linear algebra problems to playing with friends. My father (Baba) even paid me to go outside and play, hoping to encourage more conventional childhood activities. Their tolerance let me explore the mathematical topics that have long fascinated me and later helped me develop expertise in physics, statistics and artificial intelligence.

My father passed away while I was polishing the second version for Cambridge University Press. I have since taken a long break at home in Malaysia to finish this book. When I tidied up what he left behind, I found that statistics and calculus were his worst subjects at university. Perhaps this is why he paid me to go outside and play.

The dedication also extends to my grandmother (Popo), who had no formal education herself and was amused by my mathematics scribble books. When we visited, she sewed blankets while I sat in her back room solving equations. She would occasionally peek over my shoulder with curiosity and pride. Her quiet support and the warmth of those childhood memories have stayed with me throughout this journey.

Looking back, I realize that writing a textbook is itself an exercise in the kind of thinking it teaches. Like fitting a statistical model, it requires a balance of completeness and clarity, of rigor and accessibility, and of personal perspective and objective presentation. The process has taught me as much as I hope the book will teach its readers.

To those who work through this material, I hope that you learn something from it. I also hope that it changes how you think about the relationship between data and knowledge. I expect the future of astronomy to need ever more sophisticated statistical thinking. I hope that this grounding helps you, whichever specific techniques prove most useful for your research problems.

The conversation about machine learning in astronomy is far from over. It should continue to evolve as our computing power and our theoretical understanding grow. What matters most is that it rests on careful thinking. We need to ask what we are trying to achieve and why some approaches reach those goals better than others.

Thank you for joining me on this journey through statistical machine learning for astronomy. The real work begins when you close this book and start applying these ideas to your own research questions.
